Asymptotic Study of In-context Learning with Random Transformers through Equivalent Models

We acknowledge that this work is supported partially by TÜBİTAK under project 124E063 in ARDEB 1001 program. S.D. is supported by an AI Fellowship provided by KUIS AI Research Center and a PhD Scholarship (BİDEB 2211) from TÜBİTAK. The corresponding author is Zafer Doğan (zdogan@ku.edu.tr).
Abstract

We study the in-context learning (ICL) capabilities of pretrained Transformers in the setting of nonlinear regression. Specifically, we focus on a random Transformer with a nonlinear MLP head where the first layer is randomly initialized and fixed while the second layer is trained. Furthermore, we consider an asymptotic regime where the context length, input dimension, hidden dimension, number of training tasks, and number of training samples jointly grow. In this setting, we show that the random Transformer behaves equivalent to a finite-degree Hermite polynomial model in terms of ICL error. This equivalence is validated through simulations across varying activation functions, context lengths, hidden layer widths (revealing a double-descent phenomenon), and regularization settings. Our results offer theoretical and empirical insights into when and how MLP layers enhance ICL, and how nonlinearity and over-parameterization influence model performance.

Samet Demir,  Zafer Doğan
MLIP Research Group, KUIS AI Center & Department of EEE, Koç University
İstanbul, Turkey

Index Terms—  In-context learning, transformer, deep learning theory, high-dimensional asymptotics.

1 Introduction

Transformers [1] have become the backbone of deep learning in recent years. One of their emerging capabilities is the so-called in-context learning (ICL), which enables task adaptation from prompts without modifying internal parameters [2]. Given the popularity and effectiveness of Transformers for ICL, a theoretical understanding of their ICL capabilities has become a subject of significant interest.

Due to the complexity of analyzing ICL in full generality, existing studies often consider simplified settings. In particular, many works focus on ICL in linear regression or classification tasks using Transformer models stripped down to attention-only architectures, omitting multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) entirely [3, 4, 5, 6]. While recent studies have begun exploring the role of nonlinear MLPs in Transformer-based ICL [7, 8, 9], several limitations remain. For example, [7] focuses specifically on classification tasks with ReLU-based MLPs, without considering broader activation functions or regression tasks. Meanwhile, [8, 9] analyze Transformer variants in which the MLP layers precede the attention mechanism—contrary to the original Transformer architecture [1], where input embeddings first pass through attention blocks before being processed by MLPs. As a result, a comprehensive understanding of how MLPs affect ICL performance in standard Transformer architectures remains incomplete.

To address this gap, we investigate the ICL performance of Transformers with nonlinear MLPs for nonlinear regression tasks through the lens of asymptotic analysis. Our approach bridges two research areas: ICL by Transformers and the asymptotic theory of MLPs. For the latter, we draw on Gaussian universality results [10, 11, 12], which show that certain classes of MLPs are equivalent in behavior to Gaussian models with matched moments. This equivalence enables us to characterize the influence of nonlinear MLPs on the ICL performance of Transformers.

Concretely, we consider a random Transformer model with linear attention and a nonlinear MLP, where the first layer weights of the MLP are randomly initialized and fixed while the second layer is fully trained. In this setting, we show that the Transformer is asymptotically equivalent to a finite-degree polynomial model in terms of in-context learning error. We also identify the conditions under which the presence of a nonlinear MLP leads to improved ICL performance over a Transformer without MLPs. Specifically, our findings indicate that MLPs enhance ICL when the following conditions are met: (i) the activation function is appropriately chosen, (ii) the context length is sufficiently large, and (iii) the hidden dimension is suitably selected or the model is properly regularized. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the ICL error of Transformers with nonlinear MLPs may exhibit non-monotonic behavior—commonly referred to as the ”double-descent phenomenon”—as a function of model complexity. This extends prior observations of double descent in MLPs [13, 14] to the ICL setting.

Overall, our contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We find a polynomial model that performs equivalent to the random Transformer with MLPs for ICL.

  2. 2.

    We characterize the conditions under which the Transformer with nonlinear MLPs outperforms the Transformer without MLPs.

  3. 3.

    We demonstrate that non-monotonic behavior appearing in the ICL error of the Transformer with MLP can be mitigated with proper regularization.

2 Related Work: ICL with Transformers

The seminal work of [2] first highlighted Transformers’ capacity for in-context learning, sparking a surge of empirical and theoretical investigations. On the empirical side, studies such as [15], [16], and [17] demonstrated that ICL abilities tend to emerge more prominently as model size increases, emphasizing its significance in large-scale AI systems. To better understand the mechanisms behind ICL, researchers have employed controlled synthetic benchmarks, most notably linear regression tasks, using Transformers as in [6], [18], and [19]. These benchmarks enable precise analysis by isolating specific architectural and data-driven effects.

Theoretically, numerous works have proposed that Transformers implicitly acquire algorithmic structures during pretraining, which are subsequently applied during ICL [20, 21, 3, 22, 4, 23, 24, 6, 25, 26]. However, the exact nature of these learned algorithms remains an open question. To gain tractability, many of these studies analyze simplified Transformer models—especially those with linearized self-attention. In particular, [6] and [27, 28] provide detailed generalization analysis for linear attention-based Transformers in synthetic ICL tasks.

More recently, the inclusion of nonlinear MLP components in Transformer architectures has attracted attention. For example, [7] investigated ICL in a classification setting with ReLU-based MLP, while [8] and [9] examined models where the MLP layer precedes the attention mechanism. However, these works either restrict the choice of activation function and task type or depart from the standard Transformer architecture [1], where attention layers precede MLPs.

Consequently, a comprehensive theoretical treatment of ICL in Transformers with nonlinear MLP heads—adhering to the original architecture and applicable to general task settings such as regression—remains absent from the literature. This is the gap that our work seeks to address.

3 Setting

In this work, we investigate the ICL capabilities of pretrained Transformer architectures on nonlinear regression problems.

Specifically, given a sequence of paired examples

(𝒙1,y1),(𝒙2,y2),…,(𝒙ℓ,yℓ),(𝒙ℓ+1,?),\bigl({\bm{x}}_{1},y_{1}\bigr),\,\bigl({\bm{x}}_{2},y_{2}\bigr),\dots,\bigl({\bm{x}}_{\ell},y_{\ell}\bigr),\,({\bm{x}}_{\ell+1},\,?),

with each input 𝒙i∈ℝd{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and corresponding scalar response yi∈ℝy_{i}\in\mathbb{R} drawn independently from an unknown joint distribution, the model must infer the underlying mapping from the first ℓ\ell examples and predict the label yℓ+1y_{\ell+1} for a new input 𝒙ℓ+1{\bm{x}}_{\ell+1}. Here, ℓ\ell denotes the context length.

We posit a nonlinear relationship between 𝒙{\bm{x}} and yy governed by a context-specific parameter vector 𝝃∈ℝd\bm{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, subject to additive Gaussian noise. Although 𝝃\bm{\xi} remains constant within a given context, it is resampled across different contexts, imposing the requirement that the model estimate 𝝃\bm{\xi} from the observed pairs before generalizing to the new input. Formally, we generate data according to

𝒙i∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d/d),yi=σ∗​(𝝃T​𝒙i)+ϵi,\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}_{d}/d\bigr),\quad y_{i}=\sigma_{*}\bigl(\bm{\xi}^{T}{\bm{x}}_{i}\bigr)+\epsilon_{i}, (1)

where σ∗:ℝ→ℝ\sigma_{*}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is a nonlinear function and ϵi∼𝒩⁡(0,ρ)\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\rho) for ρ>0\rho>0, while the task vector itself is drawn as

𝝃∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d).\displaystyle\bm{\xi}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}_{d}\bigr). (2)

This probabilistic formulation captures both the nonlinear dependency and the variability inherent in regression tasks. We then consider kk random task vectors 𝝃{\bm{\xi}} to be used to generate the training samples, while the in-context learning error is measured with an expectation over all possible task vectors.

To feed these examples into a Transformer, we follow the literature [6] and form an embedding matrix 𝒁{\bm{Z}} by stacking the feature vectors atop their scalar labels (with a zero placeholder for the final label), namely

𝒁=[𝒙1𝒙2⋯𝒙ℓ𝒙ℓ+1y1y2⋯yℓ0]∈ℝ(d+1)×(ℓ+1).\displaystyle{\bm{Z}}\;=\;\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{x}}_{1}&{\bm{x}}_{2}&\cdots&{\bm{x}}_{\ell}&{\bm{x}}_{\ell+1}\\[3.0pt] y_{1}&y_{2}&\cdots&y_{\ell}&0\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times(\ell+1)}. (3)

The Transformer must leverage this representation to infer the underlying nonlinear mapping and accurately predict yℓ+1y_{\ell+1}. Then, the output of linear attention in the Transformer can be calculated as follows:

𝑨:=𝒁+1ℓ​𝑽​𝒁​(𝑲​𝒁)T​(𝑸​𝒁),\displaystyle{\bm{A}}:={\bm{Z}}+\frac{1}{\ell}{\bm{V}}{\bm{Z}}({\bm{K}}{\bm{Z}})^{T}({\bm{Q}}{\bm{Z}}), (4)

where 𝑲,𝑸,𝑽{\bm{K}},{\bm{Q}},{\bm{V}} are appropriately sized key, query, and value matrices, respectively. When predicting yℓ+1y_{\ell+1}, the relevant output of the attention is Ad+1,ℓ+1A_{d+1,\ell+1}. Thus, we consider the prediction of linear Transformer (without MLPs) as

y^l​i​n​e​a​r:=Ad+1,ℓ+1.\displaystyle\hat{y}_{linear}:=A_{d+1,\ell+1}. (5)

This prediction can be simplified to the following form using the reparameterization technique used by [27, 28]:

y^l​i​n​e​a​r=vec​(𝚪)T​vec​(𝑯𝒁),\displaystyle\hat{y}_{linear}=\text{vec}({\bm{\Gamma}})^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}}), (6)

where vec​(⋅)\text{vec}(\cdot) denotes the vectorization operation, 𝚪∈ℝd×(d+1){\bm{\Gamma}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times(d+1)} is the parameter matrix formed using the entries of 𝑽,𝑲,𝑸{\bm{V}},{\bm{K}},{\bm{Q}} matrices while 𝑯𝒁{\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}} is defined as

𝑯𝒁:=𝒙ℓ+1​[dℓ​∑i≤ℓyi​𝒙iT1ℓ​∑i≤ℓyi2]∈ℝd×(d+1).\displaystyle{\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}}:={\bm{x}}_{\ell+1}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{d}{\ell}\sum_{i\leq\ell}y_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i}^{T}&\frac{1}{\ell}\sum_{i\leq\ell}y_{i}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times(d+1)}.

Note that 𝚪{\bm{\Gamma}} is trained for the linear Transformer case as

arg​min𝚪∑j=1n(yℓ+1j−vec(𝚪)Tvec(𝐇𝐙j))2+λnd∥𝚪∥F2,\displaystyle\argmin_{{\bm{\Gamma}}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(y_{\ell+1}^{j}-\text{vec}({\bm{\Gamma}})^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}^{j}})\right)^{2}+\lambda\frac{n}{d}\|{\bm{\Gamma}}\|_{F}^{2},

where λ\lambda is the regularization constant, n/dn/d factor next to λ\lambda is used to keep the regularization meaningful in the asymptotic regime we consider. Here, {(𝒁j,yℓ+1j)}j=1n\{({\bm{Z}}^{j},y_{\ell+1}^{j})\}_{j=1}^{n} denotes the nn samples used for the training where 𝒁j{\bm{Z}}^{j} is formed by (3).

For the Transformer with a nonlinear MLP, the prediction of the model can be similarly written as

y^n​o​n​l​i​n​e​a​r:=𝒘T​σ​(𝑭T​vec​(𝑯𝒁)),\displaystyle\hat{y}_{nonlinear}:={\bm{w}}^{T}\sigma({\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}})), (7)

where σ:ℝ→ℝ\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is the activation function of the nonlinear MLP. Motivated by the random feature model [29, 10], we consider 𝑭∈ℝd⁡(d+1)×m{\bm{F}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d(d+1)\times m} that is randomly initialized and fixed, while similar to the training above, the parameter vector 𝒘∈ℝm{\bm{w}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is trained as

arg​min𝐰∑j=1n(yℓ+1j−𝐰Tσ(𝐅Tvec(𝐇𝐙j)))2+λnd∥𝐰∥22.\displaystyle\argmin_{{\bm{w}}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(y_{\ell+1}^{j}-{\bm{w}}^{T}\sigma({\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}^{j}}))\right)^{2}+\lambda\frac{n}{d}\|{\bm{w}}\|_{2}^{2}.

Then, we measure the ICL error with

𝔼(𝝃,𝒁,yℓ+1)​[(yℓ+1−y^)2],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{({\bm{\xi}},{\bm{Z}},y_{\ell+1})}\left[\left(y_{\ell+1}-\hat{y}\right)^{2}\right], (8)

where y^\hat{y} refers to (6) for the linear Transformer or it denotes (7) for the Transformer with a nonlinear MLP.

4 Main Results

In this work, we characterize the ICL error (8) for the Transformer with a nonlinear MLP in an asymptotic regime. Namely, we assume that the input dimension dd, the number of training samples nn, the number of task vectors used in training kk, the context length ℓ\ell, and the hidden dimension mm jointly diverge while ℓ/d,k/d,n/d2,m/n\ell/d,k/d,n/d^{2},m/n stay constants. Here, the first three scalings have been identified by [27, 28] for ICL with the linear Transformer, while the last scaling ensures that the model complexity and the training samples are comparable, as assumed typically in the literature [10].

We start our analysis with an equivalent statistical representation of the random feature mapping 𝑭T​vec​(𝑯𝒁){\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}) in the following lemma. We later utilize it to analyze the Transformer with a nonlinear MLP (7).

Lemma 1 (Asymptotic Distribution of 𝑭T​vec​(𝑯𝒁){\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}})).


Suppose the entries of 𝐅{\bm{F}} are independent and identically distributed as 𝒩⁡(0,1/tr​(Cov​(vec​(𝐇𝐙))))\mathcal{N}(0,1/\text{tr}(\text{Cov}(\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}})))) so that elements of 𝐅T​vec​(𝐇𝐙){\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}) have unit variance, where tr(.)\text{tr}(.) and Cov(.)\text{Cov}(.) denote the trace and covariance operators. Let 𝐟i{\bm{f}}_{i} denote the ii-th column of 𝐅{\bm{F}}. As l,d→∞l,d\to\infty with l/d∈ℝ+l/d\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, we have

𝒇iT​vec​(𝑯𝒁)→𝒩⁡(0,1)​ almost surely,\displaystyle{\bm{f}}_{i}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}})\to\mathcal{N}(0,1)\textit{ almost surely,} (9)

for all i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\dots,m\}.

Proof.

Let t:=tr​(Cov​(vec​(𝑯𝒁)))t:=\text{tr}(\text{Cov}(\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}))). For a given 𝑯𝒁{\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}}, the conditional distribution of 𝒇iT​vec​(𝑯𝒁){\bm{f}}_{i}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}}) is

𝒇iT​vec​(𝑯𝒁)|𝑯𝒁∼𝒩⁡(0,‖vec​(𝑯𝒁)‖22/t).\displaystyle{\bm{f}}_{i}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}})\mid{\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\|\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}})\|_{2}^{2}/t). (10)

Then, by the concentration of ‖vec​(𝑯𝒁)‖22/t\|\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}})\|_{2}^{2}/t around 11, we reach the statement of the lemma. ∎

This lemma enables us to simplify the term 𝑭T​vec​(𝑯𝒁){\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}), facilitating its use in our analysis of in-context learning with Transformers. Consequently, we shift our focus to the joint distribution of (𝑭T​vec​(𝑯𝒁),𝝃T​𝒙ℓ+1)({\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}),\,\bm{\xi}^{T}{\bm{x}}_{\ell+1}) rather than (𝑯𝒁,yℓ+1)({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}},\,y_{\ell+1}), since yℓ+1=σ∗​(𝝃T​𝒙ℓ+1)+ϵℓ+1y_{\ell+1}=\sigma_{*}(\bm{\xi}^{T}{\bm{x}}_{\ell+1})+\epsilon_{\ell+1} by (1). The following establishes that the pair (𝑭T​vec​(𝑯𝒁),𝝃T​𝒙ℓ+1)({\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}),\,\bm{\xi}^{T}{\bm{x}}_{\ell+1}) converges in distribution to a jointly Gaussian random vector in the high-dimensional limit.

Corollary 2 (Joint Distribution of (𝑭T​vec​(𝑯𝒁),𝝃T​𝒙ℓ+1)({\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}),{\bm{\xi}}^{T}{\bm{x}}_{\ell+1})).

Suppose that the task vector 𝛏{\bm{\xi}} is given. Under the assumptions of Lemma 1, as l,d→∞l,d\to\infty with l/d∈ℝ+l/d\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, (𝐅T​vec​(𝐇𝐙),𝛏T​𝐱ℓ+1)({\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}),{\bm{\xi}}^{T}{\bm{x}}_{\ell+1}) becomes jointly Gaussian with zero mean and some covariance. Here, the joint distribution appears since the construction of vec​(𝐇𝐙)\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}) includes 𝐱ℓ+1{\bm{x}}_{\ell+1}.

Lemmas 1 and Corollary 2 collectively characterize the distributions of both the input vec​(𝑯𝒁)\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{{\bm{Z}}}) of the nonlinear MLP and the label yℓ+1y_{\ell+1}. With these components established, we can now leverage the preceding results in conjunction with existing asymptotic analyses of two-layer neural networks [11, 12] to study the in-context learning error defined in (8) for Transformers equipped with nonlinear MLPs. The following theorem identifies a model that is asymptotically equivalent to such a Transformer architecture, where “asymptotic equivalence” is defined as both models achieving the same ICL error (8) in the asymptotic limit that we consider in this work.

Theorem 3 (Equivalent Polynomial Model).

Consider the setting in Lemma 1, where d,n,m,ℓ,kd,n,m,\ell,k jointly diverge with ℓ/d,k/d,n/d2,m/n∈ℝ+\ell/d,k/d,n/d^{2},m/n\in\mathbb{R}^{+}. Assume further that σ\sigma and σ∗\sigma_{*} are Lipschitz functions satisfying 𝔼x∼𝒩⁡(0,1)​[σ​(x)2]<∞\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\sigma(x)^{2}]<\infty, which ensures the existence of a Hermite expansion. Then, the Transformer with a nonlinear MLP in (7) is asymptotically equivalent—in terms of ICL error—to the following model:

𝒘T​σ^r​(𝑭T​vec​(𝑯𝒁)).\displaystyle{\bm{w}}^{T}\hat{\sigma}_{r}({\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}})). (11)

Here, σ^r:ℝ→ℝ\hat{\sigma}_{r}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is a degree-rr polynomial function with a residual term, which is defined as

σ^r​(x):=∑i=0r1i!​ci​H​ei​(x)+cr∗​z,z∼𝒩⁡(0,1),\displaystyle\hat{\sigma}_{r}(x):=\sum_{i=0}^{r}\frac{1}{i!}c_{i}He_{i}(x)+c_{r}^{*}z,\quad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), (12)

where H​ei:ℝ→ℝHe_{i}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} denotes the ii-th (probabilist’s) Hermite polynomial, cic_{i} are the corresponding Hermite coefficients and cr∗c_{r}^{*} is the residual term such that 𝔼x∼𝒩⁡(0,1)​[σ^r​(x)2]=𝔼x∼𝒩⁡(0,1)​[σ​(x)2]\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\hat{\sigma}_{r}(x)^{2}]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\sigma(x)^{2}]. The degree rr depends on both σ\sigma and the joint distribution of (𝐅T​vec​(𝐇𝐙),𝛏T​𝐱ℓ+1)({\bm{F}}^{T}\text{vec}({\bm{H}}_{\bm{Z}}),\,{\bm{\xi}}^{T}{\bm{x}}_{\ell+1}), but empirically a small finite rr suffices.

Proof.

The orthogonality of Hermite polynomials with respect to the Gaussian measure can be utilized together with the Corollary 2 to prove this theorem, which is omitted here. For an example of such a proof, we refer to [12]. ∎

Theorem 3 establishes an equivalent yet analytically tractable model for studying random Transformers equipped with a nonlinear MLP for in-context learning. Leveraging this equivalent formulation, we proceed to systematically compare the performance of the Transformer with a nonlinear MLP against that of the linear Transformer. Additionally, we empirically validate the equivalence between the nonlinear MLP Transformer and its polynomial surrogate, highlighting the predictive alignment of the two models under various conditions.

Figure 1 illustrates how the ICL error evolves with the number of training samples nn. Firstly, a non-monotonic trend is observed due to a relatively small regularization constant. Notably, the ICL errors of the equivalent polynomial model (from Theorem 3) match those of the Transformer model, confirming our theoretical findings. Furthermore, similar to the case for supervised learning with two-layer neural networks [11], ICL performance of the Transformer model is affected by the relationship between the activation function σ\sigma and the target function σ∗\sigma_{*} based on their Hermite expansions (coefficients), which is illustrated in Figure 1a-b. In Figure 1(a), across all values of nn, the Transformer augmented with a nonlinear MLP head (using ReLU activation) consistently achieves lower ICL error than the linear Transformer baseline. This performance gap underscores the benefit of nonlinear feature processing in this regime. In contrast, the MLP with tanh activation offers limited or no improvement over the linear model, suggesting that the effectiveness of nonlinear heads is highly sensitive to the choice of activation function. When the underlying target function is itself a tanh (Figure 1(b)), the performance gains from using an MLP diminish. The tanh-activated Transformer achieves only marginal improvements over the linear baseline, indicating that alignment between the MLP activation and the true task nonlinearity plays a critical role. These results suggest that MLP layers are most beneficial when their nonlinearities match or complement the structure of the target function.

Figure 2 illustrates the effect of various parameters on the ICL error while confirming that the polynomial model’s ICL performance matches that of the random Transformer model. First, in Figure 2(a), we study the effect of the context length ℓ\ell on the ICL error, indicating that increasing the context length uniformly reduces the ICL error for all models. Crucially, once the context length exceeds a threshold (ℓ≈d\ell\approx d in our setup), the Transformer with an MLP head begins to significantly outperform the linear Transformer. This observation highlights the importance of prompt richness: a sufficiently long context is necessary for the nonlinear MLP components to extract and leverage higher-order statistical structure effectively. Next, in Figure 2(b), the dependence of performance on the hidden dimension mm reveals a characteristic non-monotonic behavior commonly known as “double-descent phenomenon”: the ICL error decreases in the under-parameterized regime, peaks near the interpolation threshold (m/n≈1m/n\approx 1), and then declines again as the model enters the over-parameterized regime. This pattern emphasizes the importance of choosing the MLP width carefully. Optimal results are achieved in the suitably over-parameterized regime, where the model can fully exploit nonlinear adaptation capabilities. Finally, regularization (in Figure 2(c)) mitigates this non-monotonic behavior by smoothing the sharp peak near the interpolation threshold. As the regularization strength λ\lambda increases, the curve becomes more stable and the error peak is attenuated. These results confirm that proper regularization is essential for mitigating the double-descent phenomenon [13].

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we presented a high-dimensional analysis of in-context learning (ICL) for Transformers equipped with a nonlinear MLP head. By leveraging tools from Gaussian universality and Hermite polynomial expansions, we proved that a randomly initialized Transformer with an MLP head is asymptotically equivalent to a finite-degree polynomial model. Our theoretical findings precisely delineate the regimes in which nonlinear feature processing provides significant improvements over purely linear attention mechanisms. Extensive simulations support our theory, demonstrating that: (i) the MLP head significantly reduces ICL error when the target function is nonlinear; (ii) the benefits of the MLP emerge only when the context length exceeds certain dimension-dependent thresholds; and (iii) the model’s ICL error exhibits a double-descent behavior with respect to complexity, which can be effectively mitigated through appropriate regularization.

These results not only deepen our theoretical understanding of how nonlinearity and over-parameterization affect ICL but also offer practical guidance for designing Transformer architectures with MLP layers. Future directions include extending the analysis to multi-head attention, exploring deep stacking of MLP blocks, and developing adaptive regularization schemes tailored to the interpolation regime.
